newsitem.title: UGANDA: Uganda's Museveni sees slower economic growth.
newsitem.headline: Uganda's Museveni sees slower economic growth.

text.p: Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni said he had discovered huge fraud in an audit of the army fighting an uprising in the north and sharply criticised corrupt officials as partly responsible for growth setbacks.
Museveni told parliament that Uganda lost 400 million shillings ($400,000) per month in the north Gulu barracks as pay to "ghost" soldiers. He said that the paymaster in charge had committed suicide.
Museveni would not say for how long the fraud existed.

Museveni spoke on Monday after International Monetary Fund (IMF) policy development and review department director said the IMF would look closely at Uganda's military spending in talks due this summer on an IMF-backed economic reform package.
In Washington, the IMF's Jack Boorman told a news conference: "I am sure the budgetary burden of military spending on Uganda will be a subject in the forthcoming negotiations."

The IMF is to negotiate the renewal of a three-year plan of economic reforms with Uganda this summer. That programme opens the way to debt reduction, and can encourage investment and aid flows by underpinning international confidence.

Museveni told parliament Uganda was a star economic performer by any standards but there was potential to do better. He said he was concerned some civil servants were lax, corrupt and incompetent, which undermined overall economic growth.
He forecast economic growth at 7.0 percent in 1997 from a figure of 8.3 percent in 1996 and saw inflation maintained in the single digit range, which now stands at 7.0 percent.

Museveni said earnings from exports would reach $1.4 billion while grants would bring in another $578.35 million. He did not give a specific figure for earnings from coffee exports, which account for some 64 percent of Uganda's hard currency receipts.
He said Uganda would collect around 828 billion shillings in taxes in 1996/97 or 11 percent of gross domestic product (GDP). He did not provide comparative figures for the previous year.

On privatisation of state enterprises, Museveni said that from an initial list of 107, some 67 had already been sold. But he did not speak of the progress in privatising the big state companies, such as Uganda Posts and Telecommunications Corp.

Museveni said that under the government's universal primary education (UPE) programme, under which the state funds primary education for up to four children per family, 6.6 million pupils would be enrolled in primary schools from 5.7 million in 1997.
Last year, there were 2.9 million primary school children.
"We have been encouraged by the response of Ugandans towards universal primary education programme," Museveni said.
Museveni said Uganda had recalled retired teachers because of the programme -- because some 143,591 teachers were required against a current total of 50,973.
